title: ECDSA
summary: ECDSA is the elliptic curve analogue of the Digital Signature Algorithm, producing signatures whose security depends on the hardness of the elliptic curve discrete logarithm problem rather than integer factorisation. A signature is generated from a private scalar, a per-signature secret nonce, and the message hash; verification uses the public point and the curve parameters. Because the security per bit is higher than RSA, ECDSA keys are far smaller for equivalent strength, which is why it dominates TLS certificates, code signing, SSH keys and hardware-backed authentication on mobile devices. The critical operational property is that the nonce must be unique and unpredictable for every signature made with a given private key. Reusing a nonce across two signatures over different messages allows the private key to be recovered algebraically from the two signatures alone, and this is not a theoretical concern: it has happened repeatedly through flawed random number generation and through code paths that derive the nonce deterministically but incorrectly. Other practical hazards include weak or duplicated entropy on embedded devices, curve parameters that are not the standardised NIST or Curve25519 family, malleable signature encodings that break naive transaction or protocol logic, and libraries that accept a public key without validating that it lies on the curve. Defensive practice therefore centres on vetted libraries, deterministic nonce generation, hardware key storage, and inventorying where signatures are produced.
objectives: Explain how ECDSA signing and verification use the curve, the private scalar and the per-signature nonce.
Describe how nonce reuse across two signatures reveals a private key and what evidence of that failure looks like.
Compare ECDSA key sizes and performance with RSA and state where each is still the better operational choice.
Validate curve parameters and public key encoding during a review of a signature verification implementation.
Recognise malleable signature encodings and explain why canonicalisation matters to protocol logic.
Plan a migration from classic curves to modern alternatives while preserving certificate and key continuity.

sources.label: NIST SP 800-57 Part 1: Recommendation for Key Management

beginner.definition: ECDSA stands for Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm. It is a way to prove that a message really came from you and was not changed on the way. You keep a private key secret and share a public key. The maths works with points on a curve.
beginner.whyItMatters: Digital signatures are how software, websites and messages prove their origin. ECDSA gives you the same trust as older methods but with much smaller keys. Smaller keys mean faster connections and less storage, which matters on phones and small devices. It also has one strict rule: the secret value used for each signature must never repeat.
howItWorks: You create a key pair. The private key stays with you and the public key is shared openly.
To sign a message, you first hash it, which turns it into a short fixed value.
You combine that hash with your private key and a fresh random number for this signature.
The result is a signature that only your private key could have produced.
Anyone with your public key can check the signature against the same message hash.
If the random number is ever reused, an attacker can work out your private key.
beginner.example: Think of a special pen that only you own. When you sign a document, the ink changes shape depending on the exact paper and the exact time. Anyone can look at the signature and the document and confirm it is genuine. But if you ever sign two documents at the same recorded moment, anyone can copy your pen. That moment is the random number, and it must always be different.
takeaways: ECDSA proves who sent a message using a small, efficient key pair.
Each signature needs a fresh random value. Reusing it exposes your private key.
Use a well-tested library, because this maths is very easy to get wrong by hand.
